passage: My name is Kavitha, and last month Ayaan sat with me for an hour in the colony park and explained my Hindi homework until I finally understood it. I was so grateful. So when our unit test came and Ayaan whispered, "Remember what I did? Show me your answers," my stomach dropped. I did owe Ayaan something, that was true. But copying would put us both in trouble. I said, "I can't do that. But come to my house after school and I'll go through the chapter with you, like you did for me." Ayaan was a bit sulky, but he came over on Saturday. We spent the afternoon on the chapter, and by the end the sulking was gone.

qa.q: Where did Ayaan help Kavitha with the Hindi homework?
qa.a: Ayaan helped Kavitha in the colony park.

qa.q: What was Kavitha feeling when Ayaan whispered the request?
qa.a: Kavitha's stomach dropped: Kavitha felt pulled between gratitude for the help and knowing that copying would put both of them in trouble.

qa.q: How could Kavitha repay a friend who once helped?
qa.a: Kavitha could keep offering to study together, like going through the chapter after school.

qa.q: How might Ayaan have seen Kavitha's refusal?
qa.a: At first perhaps let down, as the sulky reaction shows, but the offer to study together may have shown that Kavitha still valued the friendship.

grounding: Illustrates a child who is grateful to a friend yet refuses to help him cheat and repays honestly.

passage:
Two weeks ago. Saurabh was stuck on his Hindi essay the night before it was due, and Tejas came over and helped him plan it, sentence by sentence. Saurabh was so grateful he said, 'I owe you big.'
Monday. Before the science test, Tejas whispered, 'Remember you owe me? Pass me your answer sheet when Sir turns round.' Saurabh's stomach dropped. He did owe Tejas. Didn't he?
Tuesday. Saurabh had kept his sheet covered in the test, and Tejas wouldn't look at him. At break Saurabh went over. 'I'm grateful, really. But I won't help you cheat. I'll help you revise for the retest, every evening this week. That's how I pay you back.' Tejas kicked at the gravel, hands in his pockets, then shrugged. 'Evenings at your place. Your mum makes better snacks.'

qa.q: What did Tejas help Saurabh with two weeks ago?
What was Saurabh feeling when Tejas said 'Remember you owe me'?
qa.a: Torn and uneasy; his stomach dropped because he felt indebted but knew cheating was wrong.

qa.q: How did Saurabh repay Tejas honestly?
qa.a: He refused to pass his answer sheet but offered to help Tejas revise every evening for the retest.

qa.q: How did Tejas feel after Saurabh kept his sheet covered?
qa.a: Annoyed or hurt; he wouldn't look at Saurabh.

grounding: A boy who owes his friend a favour refuses to help him cheat and repays him with honest help instead.

passage: 'Siddharth, your friend says you owe him? Let your Amandeep Chacha tell you about Gurnam. When I was eleven, my bat broke before the inter-school match, and Gurnam lent me his, the best bat in the village. I scored my first fifty with it. I felt I owed him forever. Then, in the half-yearly exam, he pushed a chit towards me: "Write the answers for me. You owe me." My hands went cold. I did owe him. But not that. I shook my head and kept my eyes on my own paper. After school I carried his bat to his house and said, "Every Sunday, you and me, your weak subjects." He was angry for a week. Then he came on Sunday.'

qa.q: What did Gurnam lend young Amandeep?
qa.a: His bat, the best bat in the village.

qa.q: What was young Amandeep feeling when Gurnam pushed the chit?
qa.a: Torn and uneasy; his hands went cold because he felt he owed Gurnam but knew cheating was wrong.

qa.q: How did young Amandeep repay Gurnam in the story?
qa.a: By teaching him every Sunday instead of writing his answers.

qa.q: How did Gurnam feel about Amandeep's refusal?
qa.a: Angry for a week, then willing enough to come on Sunday.

grounding: An uncle recalls owing a friend a favour, refusing to help him cheat, and repaying him by teaching him.
